newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU raps governments' knuckles over lost money.
newsitem.headline: EU raps governments' knuckles over lost money.

text.p: The European Union's budget watchdog rapped governments on the knuckles on Tuesday for making "substantial errors" in doling out EU money and for failing to get to grips with fraud.

The EU's Court of Auditors said that on the basis of sample examinations, four billion Ecus ($5 billion) of EU cash -- almost six percent of all expenditure -- were paid out wrongly, whether to export suspect feta cheese or for non-existent olive groves.
"On the expenditure side there are too many irregularities," Bernhard Friedmann, the President of the Luxembourg-based Court, told a news conference following publication of the annual report.
He stressed that payment errors did not in themselves amount to fraud but were often the result of bungling and incompetence by different authorities in charge of distributing the money.
He put the blame firmly on national authorities -- which control 80 percent of the payments -- rather than EU authorities in Brussels.
He said 36 percent of the errors involved payments to farmers and 42 percent funds intended to help the Union's less well-off regions. But every kind of EU expenditure was affected.
In one notable case in Denmark 16 million Ecus ($19 million) were paid out in subsidies to export to Iran Danish feta cheese, which was later suspected to be sub-standard.
Danish feta cheese is already a sore point with Greece, which says feta is a national product made out of ewes milk and Denmark should not be selling it in the first place.
"There are certain quality criteria to be observed," Friedmann said, adding that the cheese was suspected of not meeting requirements on fat content.
Member states had also still failed to account for olive groves and rice fields which were being subsidised, the report said.
It said the EU had met 50 percent of costs for two aircraft to patrol EU fishing grounds to check fishing rules were being respected without looking at the cost-effectiveness of the expenditure.
Even when breaches of the fishing rules were spotted, it said, there were no penalties to deal with the breaches.
The report said it was also not always clear who were the beneficiaries of the social and regional funds.
It said millions of dollars were being lost from the EU's contributions because of lax application of legislation and lax customs checks.
The report was less damning than in previous years, a fact the EU's Budget Commissioner Erkki Liikanen said heralded the start of a successful fight against fraud and financial irregularities.
"Ships turn around slowly, but we see it is finally starting to turn," he told the parliament.
The Commission said in a statement that the mistakes did not mean the money was lost for good, as there were procedures for reclaiming it.
